lede: A matrix equation is solved the way any equation is: undo what was done to the unknown matrix. An added or subtracted matrix is undone entry by entry. A matrix that multiplies cannot be divided away, so its inverse does the undoing, written in front on both sides.
can: Solve $A + X = B$ and $A - X = B$ entry by entry, in the right direction.
Solve $AX = B$ as $X = A^{-1}B$, the inverse in front, whatever the determinant.
Clear an added matrix first, and say why a singular matrix stops the method.

text: Undo what was done to X

md: A matrix equation is solved like a number equation: do the same to both sides until $X$ is alone. An added matrix is taken away from both sides, position by position, and the direction matters: $A + X = B$ gives $X = B - A$, never $A - B$. From $A - X = B$, add $X$ to both sides first: $X = A - B$.

stem: It is given that $A + X = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & -1 \\ 4 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}5 & 2 \\ 1 & 7\end{pmatrix}$. Find $X$.

steps.decision: Take $A$ from both sides; what is left on the right is $B - A$.
Each entry of $A$ comes off the entry in the same place in $B$.
Check: $A + X$ gives $B$ back.

prompt: It is given that $X + A = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 4 \\ -2 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}6 & 3 \\ 1 & 5\end{pmatrix}$. Which matrix is $X$?
explain: Take $A$ from both sides, as step 1 of See it did, so $X = B - A$, worked position by position: top left $6 - 1 = 5$. $A - B$ reverses every sign, and $A + B$ adds where the equation needs taking away.

twin.prompt: It is given that $X + A = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 0 & 6\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 2 & 2\end{pmatrix}$. Which matrix is $X$?
twin.explain: $X = B - A$, position by position: top left $4 - 3 = 1$, top right $1 - (-2) = 3$.

optionNotes.why: That reverses every sign: the rearrangement gives B − A.
That adds A on, where it has to come off.
That is $A - B$: taking $A$ from both sides leaves $B - A$, so every sign here is reversed.
That adds $A$ on, where the equation needs it taken off.

text: When A multiplies X, use the inverse

md: In $AX = B$ the matrix $A$ multiplies $X$, and there is no dividing by a matrix. What undoes $A$ is its inverse: $A^{-1}A = I$, the identity, which acts like the number $1$. So multiply both sides by $A^{-1}$, and $X$ is left on its own.

title: Why there is no dividing by a matrix
md: For numbers, dividing by $4$ is multiplying by $\frac{1}{4}$, the number that undoes $4$. A matrix has no reciprocal, but it may have an inverse that does the same job, and only when its determinant is not zero. So the undo is multiplication by $A^{-1}$.

steps.decision: Multiply both sides by the inverse, written in front of each side.
A matrix times its own inverse is the identity matrix, $I$.
The identity changes nothing it multiplies, so $IX$ is simply $X$.

prompt: Multiplying both sides of $AX = B$ by $A^{-1}$ gives $A^{-1}AX = A^{-1}B$. What happened to $A^{-1}A$ on the way to $X = A^{-1}B$?
options: It became the identity, which leaves $X$ unchanged
answer: It became the identity, which leaves $X$ unchanged
explain: Step 2 of See it: a matrix times its own inverse is the identity, the matrix version of $1$, and step 3 used $IX = X$. It does not vanish to zero, and it is not $A$ times itself.

twin.prompt: Which matrix, multiplied in front of $LX$, leaves $X$ on its own?
twin.explain: $L^{-1}L = I$ and $IX = X$. $L$ itself would give $L^{2}X$, and there is no dividing by a matrix.

optionNotes.why: $L$ in front gives $L^{2}X$; only the inverse undoes $L$.
There is no dividing by a matrix; its inverse does that job.
A matrix times its own inverse is the identity, not the zero matrix; zero would wipe X out.
$A^{-1}A$ is the inverse times the matrix, not $A$ times $A$: the inverse undoes $A$.

md: The inverse goes in front of $A$, where it meets $A$ and makes $I$, so it goes in front of $B$ as well: the same thing, in the same place, on both sides. The place matters because two matrices multiplied the other way round usually give a different matrix, so $BA^{-1}$ is not the answer.

steps.decision: Row by column, with the inverse first.
The same two matrices the other way round: a different matrix.
Only the inverse-first product gives $Q$ back, with $P = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, so $X = P^{-1}Q$.

prompt: To solve $LX = M$ for $X$, where must $L^{-1}$ be written?
options: In front of the left side only
explain: In front of $L$, so that $L^{-1}L$ becomes $I$, and in the same place on the right to keep the sides equal, which is the product step 3 of See it checked: $X = L^{-1}M$. Behind $L$ the inverse never meets it, so $X$ is never freed.

twin.prompt: Multiplying both sides of $LX = M$ by $L^{-1}$, which product is $X$?
twin.explain: The inverse goes in front on both sides, so the right side becomes $L^{-1}M$. $ML^{-1}$ is the other order, usually a different matrix.

optionNotes.why: That is the other order, usually a different matrix: the inverse goes in front.
One inverse in front of each side is all it takes; nothing multiplies on the right.
Behind $L$ the inverse never meets it, so $L^{-1}L$ is never formed and $X$ is not freed.

optionNotes.option: In front of the left side only
optionNotes.why: Whatever is done to one side is done to the other, in the same place, or the equation breaks.

stem: It is given that $AX = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}5 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{pmatrix}$. Find $X$.

steps.decision: The determinant first, on its own line; it is not zero, so the inverse exists.
Swap the leading diagonal, change the signs of the other two, divide by 1.
The inverse in front of $B$; $X$ will be a column, like $B$.
Each row of the inverse meets the column. Check: $AX$ gives $B$ back.

title: Matrix Equations part 1 - Corbettmaths
why: The same method on several equations, the inverse written in front each time, beside our own steps above.

prompt: It is given that $AX = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 2 \\ 4 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}5 \\ 6\end{pmatrix}$. What is the top entry of $X$?
explain: As in steps 1 to 4 of See it: $\det A = 9 - 8 = 1$, so $A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -4 & 3\end{pmatrix}$. Row 1 times the column: $3 \times 5 + (-2) \times 6 = 3$.

twin.prompt: It is given that $AX = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}7 \\ 4\end{pmatrix}$. What is the top entry of $X$?

md: Most papers set an inverse with a fraction in front, often a negative one: $\det A = -2$ gives $-\frac{1}{2}$. Keep that fraction outside the matrix. Multiply the swapped-and-negated matrix by $B$ first, in whole numbers, and divide by the determinant at the very end, minus sign included.

stem: It is given that $AX = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}5 \\ 6\end{pmatrix}$. Find $X$.

steps.decision: Negative, so the fraction in front of the inverse is negative.
Swap, change two signs, and keep $-\frac{1}{2}$ outside.
Row by column in whole numbers: $4 \times 5 + (-3) \times 6 = 2$ and $-2 \times 5 + 1 \times 6 = -4$.
Now divide by $-2$: every sign flips. Check: $AX$ gives $B$.

prompt: It is given that $AX = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{pmatrix}$. What is the top entry of $X$, as a decimal?
explain: As steps 1 to 4 of See it: $\det A = 8 - 3 = 5$. Row 1 of the swapped-and-negated matrix times the column is $4 \times 1 + (-1) \times 1 = 3$, and dividing by $5$ last gives $\frac{3}{5} = 0.6$.

twin.prompt: It is given that $AX = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 3\end{pmatrix}$. What is the top entry of $X$, as a decimal?

md: When the equation also adds or subtracts a matrix, clear that first, exactly as in a number equation: from $AX - C = B$, add $C$ to both sides to reach $AX = B + C$. Only then bring in the inverse, and let it multiply the whole of $B + C$. The papers have set this as $(P - Q)X = R$ and as $AX = B + C$.

stem: It is given that $AX - C = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, $B = \begin{pmatrix}4 \\ 3\end{pmatrix}$ and $C = \begin{pmatrix}2 \\ 5\end{pmatrix}$. Find $X$.

steps.decision: Add $C$ to both sides first; $A$ waits.
Swap and change signs; the determinant is 1.
The inverse multiplies the whole right side, bracket and all.
Row by column. Check: $AX - C$ gives $B$.

prompt: It is given that $AX + C = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}5 & 2 \\ 7 & 3\end{pmatrix}$, $C = \begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 2\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}7 \\ 6\end{pmatrix}$. What is the top entry of $X$?
explain: Clear $C$ first, as step 1 of See it did: $AX = B - C = \begin{pmatrix}6 \\ 4\end{pmatrix}$. Then $A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}3 & -2 \\ -7 & 5\end{pmatrix}$, and row 1 gives $18 - 8 = 10$. Going straight to $A^{-1}B$ solves a different equation.

twin.prompt: It is given that $AX - C = B$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, $C = \begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}6 \\ 3\end{pmatrix}$. What is the top entry of $X$?
twin.explain: Add $C$ first: $AX = B + C = \begin{pmatrix}7 \\ 4\end{pmatrix}$. Then $A^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & -1 \\ -3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$, and row 1 gives $7 - 4 = 3$.

md: **No inverse.** If the matrix multiplying $X$ has determinant $0$, it has no inverse and the equation cannot be solved this way. Say so naming the matrix: in 2023 some answers only said the matrix had no inverse, without saying which. A part may instead ask which value makes a matrix singular (2021).
**Unknown entries.** A product with letters in it (2021, 2024): multiply it out row by column, then set the matching entries equal and solve.
**Work something out first.** The right side may be a product or a square, as in $AY = B^{2}$ (2026): find it first, row by column, never by squaring each entry (2024).

stem: With $S = \begin{pmatrix}6 & 4 \\ 3 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, explain why $SX = B$ cannot be solved.

steps.decision: The determinant decides whether an inverse exists.
Name the matrix, $S$, not just 'the matrix'.

steps.working: So $SX = B$ cannot be solved by pre-multiplying
steps.decision: There is no $S^{-1}$ to put in front of both sides.

prompt: $T = \begin{pmatrix}4 & -2 \\ -6 & 3\end{pmatrix}$. Which line explains why $TX = B$ cannot be solved?
explain: As steps 1 and 2 of See it: $\det T = 12 - 12 = 0$, so $T$ has no inverse, and the line names $T$. 'The matrix has no inverse' does not say which matrix, and there is no dividing by a matrix.

twin.prompt: $U = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 6 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$. Which line explains why $UX = B$ cannot be solved?
twin.explain: $\det U = 6 - 6 = 0$, so $U$ has no inverse: name $U$ in the line.

optionNotes.why: Say which matrix: $U$ has no inverse.
Multiplying by $U$ adds a factor and cannot free $X$; $U$ has no inverse.
True, but it does not say which matrix; name $T$ as the one with no inverse.
There is no dividing by a matrix, and $T$ has no inverse to do the job either.

md:
$A + X = B$: $X = B - A$, position by position.
$AX = B$: $X = A^{-1}B$, the inverse in front of both sides.
Determinant, inverse, then the product row by column; a fraction stays outside until the end.
Clear an added matrix first, then let the inverse multiply the whole right side.
Determinant 0: name the matrix with no inverse; the equation cannot be solved this way.

Usually 4 to 7 marks, with the inverse found inside the question: marks for the determinant, the inverse, $X = A^{-1}B$ in that order, and the final matrix, whose mark needs every entry right. Stuck: write $X = A^{-1}B$ with the inverse in front; that line earns a method mark.
